passages.text: CONSUMPTION, or PHTHISIS PULMONALIS, a wasting of the body, attended with hectic fever, cough, and an expectoration of purulent matter from the lungs.
It is the most fatal of all the diseases of this climate; it has been computed that nearly one-fourth of the deaths in Britain arise from it.
On dissection the lungs are found studded with tubercles, small hard bodies which afterwards soften and form ulcers, or vomicae.
The disease is very frequently hereditary; and persons of a fair complexion, a long neck, and a narrow chest are thought especially disposed to it.
Whether it be contagious has been much disputed. In Italy and Spain the clothes of consumptive persons are burned; but in this country the opinion is generally rejected.
The stethoscope of Laennec enables the physician to detect the cavities of the lungs by the sounds of the breath and of the voice.
Change of climate, a sea voyage, exercise on horseback, and a diet of milk are recommended; but when the disease is confirmed it is seldom cured.

Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease usually caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria. It mainly affects the lungs. It was historically called consumption because of the weight loss it causes.
Active TB causes a chronic cough with blood-containing mucus, fever, night sweats and weight loss.
It spreads through the air when people with active TB in their lungs cough, speak or sneeze. Robert Koch identified the bacterium in 1882.
Most infections cause no symptoms, a state called latent tuberculosis. About one in ten latent infections progresses to active disease.
Risk factors include HIV, malnutrition, smoking, diabetes and crowded housing. Genes affect susceptibility, but the disease itself is not inherited.
The body walls off the bacteria in granulomas, small nodules called tubercles, which can break down and leave cavities in the lung.
Diagnosis relies on chest X-rays, sputum microscopy and culture, and molecular tests.
Treatment is a course of several antibiotics taken for months. Streptomycin, introduced in the 1940s, was the first effective drug. Drug-resistant TB is a growing problem.
Before antibiotics, patients were sent to sanatoria for rest, fresh air and good food.
It remains one of the leading infectious causes of death worldwide.

alignments.label: The name
alignments.note: The same disease under its old names. The modern name comes from the tubercles described on this page.

britannica.quote: hectic fever, cough, and an expectoration of purulent matter

wikipedia.quote: a chronic cough with blood-containing mucus, fever, night sweats and weight loss

alignments.label: Tubercles

britannica.quote: the lungs are found studded with tubercles

alignments.note: Same word, same finding. Wikipedia adds that they are the body walling off bacteria.

alignments.label: Is it inherited?

britannica.quote: The disease is very frequently hereditary

wikipedia.quote: the disease itself is not inherited

alignments.note: Families shared the disease because they shared air and housing, not because it was inherited.

alignments.label: Is it contagious?

britannica.quote: in this country the opinion is generally rejected

alignments.note: The biggest reversal on the page. Britain rejected contagion in 1842; Koch's bacterium settled it forty years later.

alignments.label: Can it be cured?

britannica.quote: when the disease is confirmed it is seldom cured

wikipedia.quote: Treatment is a course of several antibiotics taken for months

alignments.note: True in 1842, when there was no cure. Curable since the 1940s, though drug resistance is eroding that.

alignments.label: Rest and fresh air

britannica.quote: Change of climate, a sea voyage, exercise on horseback, and a diet of milk

wikipedia.quote: sanatoria for rest, fresh air and good food

alignments.note: Rest and food helped, but cured no one. The same regimen later moved into sanatoria.

alignments.label: Diagnosis

wikipedia.quote: chest X-rays, sputum microscopy and culture, and molecular tests

alignments.note: Listening to the chest gave way to seeing the lungs and the bacterium.

alignments.label: How deadly it is

britannica.quote: nearly one-fourth of the deaths in Britain

wikipedia.quote: one of the leading infectious causes of death worldwide

alignments.note: Still a leading killer, but no longer of Britain: the burden moved, the fact did not.

alignments.label: Who is disposed to it

britannica.quote: persons of a fair complexion, a long neck, and a narrow chest

alignments.note: This body-type profile has no place among modern risk factors.

alignments.label: Latent infection
alignments.note: Infection without disease could not be seen before the bacterium was known.

suggestedQuestions: Did people in 1842 think consumption was contagious?
Who did the 1842 entry say gets consumption, and is that still true?
How did treatment change between 1842 and today?

Did people in 1842 think consumption was.answer:
Mostly not, in Britain. The entry says contagion "has been much disputed": in Italy and Spain the clothes of consumptive people were burned, but in Britain the idea was generally rejected [B5].

Wikipedia states that the disease spreads through the air, and that Robert Koch identified the bacterium in 1882 [W3], forty years after this edition.

Who did the 1842 entry say gets consumpt.answer:
It says the disease is very often hereditary, and that people with a fair complexion, a long neck and a narrow chest are especially prone to it [B4].

Neither holds. Wikipedia lists HIV, malnutrition, smoking, diabetes and crowded housing as risk factors, and says genes affect susceptibility but the disease is not inherited [W5]. Families were sharing air, not genes, which is how the 1842 view could form from honest observation.

How did treatment change between 1842 an.answer:
In 1842 the advice was a change of climate, a sea voyage, riding and a milk diet, with the warning that confirmed cases were seldom cured [B7]. The same idea of rest and fresh air later moved into sanatoria [W9].

Real treatment arrived with antibiotics: a months-long course of several drugs, starting with streptomycin in the 1940s [W8].
